source: Dr. Thaveesak Sangudom, Dr. Theerawut Chutinanthakun, and Wirot Horasart, "Off-season Production Techniques for Pursat Orange (ក្រូចពោធិ៍សាត់ / kroch poursat) in Cambodia," in The Guideline of Climate Change Adaptation in Cambodia (pp. 130-153), Project on Promoting Climate Resilience in Farming Communities of Cambodia, General Department of Agriculture (GDA) Cambodia, Thailand International Cooperation Agency (TICA), and Department of Agriculture (DOA) Thailand, 2017-2020.
text:
Citrus Tristeza Virus (CTV) is a virus that infects the phloem tissue of citrus trees. Early leaf symptoms begin as vein-clearing (veins appearing translucent/pale against the leaf), progressing to light yellowing; affected leaves photosynthesize poorly and can curl or shrink. In heavy infections the bark and trunk develop a pitted texture known as stem-pitting, with a honeycomb-like pattern visible in the wood beneath the bark once cut into -- the source illustrates this with close-up photos of pitted stem cross-sections. Stem-pitting shows up especially in trees grafted onto sour orange rootstock. Infected trees decline in vigor, grow poorly, and produce less fruit; the source notes CTV tends to spread through an orchard faster than the other diseases covered.

Control measures given in the source:
1) Only use clean, disease-free propagation/rootstock material when establishing new trees.
2) Spray to control the insect vector: Carbaryl 85% WP at 45 g per 20 L water, or Carbosulfan at 30 ml per 20 L water.
caveat: The source's description of exactly how CTV spreads between trees (its insect vector) was on a line of dense small text that could not be read with full confidence even after repeated high-resolution zooming. Real-world citrus tristeza virus is well-established in agricultural science to spread primarily via aphids (especially the brown citrus aphid) and via infected grafting/budwood material -- this is consistent with the source's own control measures, which target clean propagation material and spray against an insect vector. That established fact is reflected in the control-measures section above, but the source's own specific wording on transmission was not fully legible and is not directly quoted.
